extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of sociology, cultural critics, and readers of Veblen's Theory of the Leisure Class
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts and systematizes the norms by which aesthetic value is formed under pecuniary (leisure-class) institutions, showing how expensiveness, social confirmation, novelty, and class habits shape judgments of beauty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dual requirement: beauty and expensiveness
rubrics_metrics.description: Any valuable object, in order to appeal to our sense of beauty, must conform to the requirements of beauty and of expensiveness both.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Veblen asserts that aesthetic appeal for the relevant social audience typically requires satisfying both ordinary aesthetic norms (form, color, proportion) and marks or signs of honorific pecuniary cost.

rubrics_metrics.name: Marks of expensiveness are assimilated into beauty
rubrics_metrics.description: The marks of expensiveness come to be accepted as beautiful features of the expensive articles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expensive attributes (gloss, rarity, costly materials) merge with 'beautiful' features in popular appreciation; e.g., patent-leather gloss read as beauty when on an expensive hat but not on a worn sleeve.

rubrics_metrics.name: Code of reputability (fashion) determines acceptable forms
rubrics_metrics.description: The code of reputability in matters of dress decides what shapes, colors, materials, and general effects in human apparel are for the time to be accepted as suitable; departures from the code are offensive to our taste.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fashion operates as a social code setting the range of 'reputably' beautiful forms; what is in vogue is sincerely pleasing to many because of this code (example: this year's fancy bonnet vs last year's).

rubrics_metrics.name: Vogue and social confirmation condition sincere liking
rubrics_metrics.description: We readily, and for the most part with utter sincerity, find those things pleasing that are in vogue; social confirmation gives tastes traction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Small or scattered elites cannot sustain taste; a class sufficiently numerous and mobile can establish 'social confirmation' so that conspicuous consumption becomes a genuine source of pleasure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expensiveness as gatekeeper: inexpensive beauty is devalued
rubrics_metrics.description: By habituation to the marks of expensiveness, a beautiful article which is not expensive is accounted not beautiful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Items that would please an untutored aesthetic sense may be rejected if they lack honorific cost—e.g., certain flowers treated as 'weeds' by upper-class schedules of pecuniary beauty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pecuniary plane/class traditions shape taste
rubrics_metrics.description: Traditions of propriety and the code of reputability are determined, more or less rigidly, by the pecuniary plane of life of the class.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Differences between classes in what counts as beautiful are not constitutional but learned via the class-specific schedule of what is honorific to consume (examples: furniture, houses, parks).

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of suggestions of thrift
rubrics_metrics.description: The vulgar suggestion of thrift is a standing objection to decorative use; appearances that connote thrift are indecorous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical, inexpensive means (e.g., grazing cattle in a lawn) may be aesthetically rejected because they suggest thrift—even if they are more 'natural' or beautiful—so expensive-looking substitutes are chosen.

rubrics_metrics.name: Studied exhibition of expensiveness under a guise of simplicity (pseudo-serviceability)
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a studious exhibition of expensiveness coupled with a make-believe of simplicity and crude serviceability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Designs often simulate rustic or serviceable forms (rustic fences, trellises, circuitous drives) while actually signaling costliness; these pseudo-serviceable devices are a class signature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Shamming serviceability as a respectable aesthetic device
rubrics_metrics.description: The middle-class affectation of serviceability works out in shamming serviceability—rustic fences, cast-iron trellises, circuitous drives—conveying the look of usefulness without thrift.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is an anti-pattern of aesthetic substitution where serviceable appearance is faked to satisfy the canon of reputable futility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preference for novelty and ingenious puzzlement as surrogate taste
rubrics_metrics.description: Where canons of conspicuous waste prevent use of simple aesthetic goods, the sense of novelty and puzzling ingenuity serves as an auxiliary sense of taste.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Objects may be designed to bewilder with irrelevant suggestions and display labor or ingenuity (feather mantles, carved ceremonial handles), substituting expensive ingenuity for straightforward beauty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beauty of form = facility of apperception (simplicity favored for true economic beauty)
rubrics_metrics.description: Beauty of form seems to be a question of facility of apperception: neat, simple, unambiguous articles best serve the aesthetic sense among objects of use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If stripped of associative or expressive elements, aesthetic beauty corresponds to how readily the mind unfolds apperceptive activity; thus true 'economic beauty' favors simplicity and clarity of function.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economic beauty: clear suggestion of adequacy to purpose
rubrics_metrics.description: Economic beauty is the expression of adequacy to a purpose—neat and unambiguous suggestion of an object's office and efficiency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For utilitarian goods, beauty arises from visible fitness for purpose; this is often suppressed by pecuniary canons that prize wasteful display instead.

rubrics_metrics.name: Substitution of expense/ingenuity often suppresses real beauty
rubrics_metrics.description: The substitution of evidences of misspent ingenuity and labor for beauty or serviceability often results in suppression of elements that would bear scrutiny as genuinely beautiful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many everyday articles, architecture, and apparel show excessive ingenuity or costly ineptitude favored for reputability rather than for aesthetic truth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Class-based mimicry: foreign upper-class standards as aesthetic exemplar
rubrics_metrics.description: Leisure-class tastes are shaped by usages apprehended to prevail among higher-ranking leisure classes (e.g., English usage), so likeness to that exemplar raises perceived beauty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A thing (e.g., a horse, trappings, horsemanship) is judged more beautiful in proportion as it is 'more English'—imitation confers reputably-correct beauty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Honorific (non-industrial) status of animals determines perceived beauty
rubrics_metrics.description: Domestic animals that ordinarily serve no industrial end (pigeons, parrots, cats, dogs, fast horses) are commonly admired and accounted beautiful because they are items of conspicuous consumption.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: By contrast, productive domestic animals (cattle, hogs, sheep) are not readily imputed beauty because they are associated with usefulness and thrift.

rubrics_metrics.name: Animal aesthetic factors: uselessness, subservience, emulation utility
rubrics_metrics.description: In animals, qualities such as wasteful uselessness, servile subservience (dog), or use as means of emulation/aggression (fast horse) contribute to their reputability and hence to their being esteemed beautiful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dogs are valued for subservience and association with the chase; race-horses are prized for emulation and display—even grotesque breeding gains aesthetic value via scarcity/expense.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ideal of human beauty shifts with economic/cultural stage
rubrics_metrics.description: The conventional ideal of feminine beauty varies by stage: robust, large-limbed women valued where service is prized; chivalric ideal of delicate, attenuated features corresponds to vicarious leisure; later shifts back under industrial development.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Economic organization and the role of women (productive vs vicarious consumer) determine which bodily traits are reputably beautiful in a society.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pecuniary norms validate artificial bodily alteration as beauty
rubrics_metrics.description: Under the canon of pecuniary decency, artificially induced pathological features (constricted waist, deformed foot) are accepted as attractive because they signal honorific nonproductivity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mutilations that are repulsive to untutored sense may be habituated into attractiveness by their status-signalling function; this is an explicit example of reputability overriding intrinsic aesthetic judgment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Confusion of reputability-value and aesthetic-value
rubrics_metrics.description: Valuation for the aesthetic purpose and for the purpose of repute are not held apart; terms commonly used to describe beauty are extended to cover reputability, producing conceptual confusion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because reputability is not linguistically distinguished, people conflate aesthetic praise with honors of pecuniary repute—this explains many misattributions of beauty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Leisure-class evolution moderates insistence on conspicuous waste
rubrics_metrics.description: As exemption from thrift becomes widespread within the leisure class, its canons of taste may relax insistence on unremitting demonstrations of expensiveness and may allow preferring rustic/natural effects (though still affected).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Newer upper-class tastes may favor 'natural' rusticity or workmanship, but these preferences are seldom wholly unaffected by honorific concerns and may still include pseudo-rustic affectations.
